article.title: Why Revenue Growth Can Produce Less Cash
article.why: Business English for separating revenue, profit, working capital, and operating cash flow.
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Revenue growth sounds like good news, but it does not automatically mean that a company is collecting more cash. Accounting revenue is recorded when a sale is recognized under the relevant rules, while cash arrives when the customer actually pays. When a business grows quickly, the gap between those two moments can become large.

Consider a company that sells ¥100 million of products this month and allows customers to pay 60 days later. Revenue may rise immediately, but much of the cash will not arrive until a future period. On the balance sheet, the unpaid amount appears as accounts receivable. If receivables grow faster than revenue, the company may be using more cash to finance its customers.

Inventory can create a second cash drain. A retailer expecting strong demand may buy goods before it sells them. Those purchases use cash now, while the related revenue may appear weeks or months later. A manufacturer can face an even longer cycle because it must buy materials, produce goods, store finished products, and then wait for customers to pay. Strong sales growth can therefore require a large investment in working capital.

This is why profit and operating cash flow can move in different directions. Profit includes revenue and expenses according to accounting recognition rules. Operating cash flow adjusts for items such as receivables, inventory, payables, and non-cash expenses. A profitable company can report weak operating cash flow when working capital absorbs cash. The reverse can also happen for a period.

Payables matter too. If a growing company receives longer payment terms from suppliers, it can delay cash outflows and partly offset the increase in receivables and inventory. But if suppliers demand faster payment, the cash pressure becomes stronger. Analysts therefore look at the whole cash conversion cycle rather than one account in isolation.

A useful review starts with three questions. First, how fast is revenue growing? Second, how fast are receivables and inventory growing? Third, is operating cash flow keeping pace with profit over several periods? A single quarter can be noisy, especially in seasonal businesses, so the trend matters more than one snapshot.

Quality of growth also matters. If management accelerates sales by offering very generous credit terms, reported revenue may improve while collection risk rises. If inventory grows because products are not selling, the company may eventually need discounts or write-downs. In both cases, the accounting result can look better before the cash reality becomes visible.

None of this means revenue growth is bad. Rapid growth often requires temporary cash investment, and that investment can be sensible when customers are reliable and margins are attractive. The key is to separate “more sales” from “more cash generated.” Revenue tells you about recognized business activity. Profit tells you what remains after recognized costs. Operating cash flow tells you how much cash the core business actually produced during the period.

When growth is strong but cash is weak, do not stop at the income statement. Trace the movement through receivables, inventory, payables, and the cash flow statement. That bridge often explains whether the company is building a healthy business, financing growth temporarily, or hiding a more serious collection and inventory problem.

Another useful measure is days sales outstanding. If customers take steadily longer to pay, rising receivables may be more than a normal effect of growth. Days inventory outstanding can reveal a similar change in stock. These ratios are not conclusions by themselves, but they help identify where to investigate the cash gap.

grammar.title: Contrast and qualification
grammar.body: Use structures such as “does not automatically mean” and “rather than” to separate related but different ideas.
